items.body: Review by alainPP — Uncompromising art rock for a fresh sound, minimalist and captivating alternative electro-prog."My Blistering Mind" boasts a distinctive sound, phrased vocals, and electronic, synth-heavy orchestration reminiscent of Porcupine Tree. A final mantra-like repetition of the gentle chorus shifts between pop, cold wave, and Bowie-esque dance-pop-rock, all set to poignant lyrics about mental fragility. "The Mandatory Prize" features a synthetic riff on electric piano, a long, melancholic, and pervasive melody set to lyrics by Dick, with a sound reminiscent of Steve Wilson. Malcolm's voice is ever-present, pale, cold, and robotic, mirroring the synth pads in a new prog style. But that riff is truly gut-wrenching. "Never Really Felt Like Home," with its ambient, hypnotic, and contemplative intro, and Kathryn's deep flute, is a symbol of tranquility. The piccolo allows for a drift into a cinematic-melancholic space where the low guitar solo amplifies this beatific, solemn instrumental. "Smile, Smile, Smile," already seen on the EP, has a haunting metronomic sound on the vibrating bass, the keyboard unfolding, flirting with Esth�sie, the addictive vocals leading to saturation. An electronic Wilson, like his side project No-Man. A stressful, redundant finale leading to musical madness through its endless repetition, the lyrics cruelly explaining this moment of schizoid disarray. "Intermission," as its name suggests, is an instrumental on bass and drums with a jazzy piano, a way of dreaming about the evolution of jazz today. The ensuing Mellotron chills the ears before the colorful piano nods to the works of Joe Jackson."Parallel Lives," with its hushed vocals and contemplative ballad-like feel, sees Kathryn's guitar work on the chorus amplify its solemnity. The effective rhythmic foundation drives this lament, reminiscent of Springsteen's "Streets of Philadelphia." The eponymous track plunges into the depths of Wavy's pop. "Eversion," one of the longer pieces, meanders with lyrics reminiscent of Kate Bush, its orchestration blending neoclassical, synth, and electronic elements, inspired by Steve Wilson. A piano and synth interlude precedes the electric return and Malcolm's vocals, sly, dark, and haughty. The guitar solo brightens the ear, and the sound returns with hypnotic, syncopated percussion, amplifying the progressive, schizophrenic feel. "Pretty Blue Fox" opens with a modern, electro-synth feel, reminiscent of Tangerine Dream in the 70s. It's a blend of electro and prog, with a satisfying mid-section, scraping away at the repetitive sounds of Philip Glass for a restrained, immersive, orgasmic finale ? pure bliss. "Just Another Thing" returns to new prog rock with its piercing, guttural vocals; you'll want to try these breathless vocalizations yourself. There's a hint of Bowie, a sound reminiscent of Simple Minds, a dynamic track with a neo-Marillion-esque keyboard solo, recounting Malcolm's retinal mishaps. "Dropping The Mask" is another instrumental with an electrified, upbeat tempo and bouncy keyboard, a nod to Tangerine Dream in the 80s ? groovy, energetic, and catchy. "Just Hold On (Pts 1 & 2)" opens with a religious, elegiac intro, the soaring choir drifting into hyperspace?a fitting way to escape this groundbreaking album. A striking mix of languid atmosphere and archaic feel, thanks to a guitar emerging from a cloud of Olympus, the solo spreading to the heavens. Malcolm finally appears on this melting synth, the drums merely controlling the rhythm. A solemn ambiance is created by the double bass, the deep vocals, the ephemeral piano, and the final, melancholic guitar outro, a meditative and hopeful finale. A truly beautiful and contemplative ending. "My Blistering Mind," in a shorter, perhaps faster version, and "The Mandatory Prize" are released as radio edits, destined for the airwaves of a better world.HATS OFF GENTLEMEN IT'S ADEQUATE blends vocal and purely instrumental tracks, delivering electronic art-rock with contemporary classical touches. A modern progressive rock sound for the new millennium. (4.5)

items._cn_summary: Hats Off Gentlemen It's Adequate 的这张专辑以简约电子化手法切入前卫摇滚领域，大量合成器编排与程式化的人声构建出冰冷、机械化的质感。主唱 Malcolm 的嗓音苍白而疏离，与合成器铺底形成统一色调，多首作品在冷波、舞曲流行与渐进摇滚之间游走。器乐段落中长笛、电钢琴、颤琴琴等元素交替出现，间奏曲目展现爵士钢琴的即兴走向。整体编曲倾向于氛围化与重复性的结构营造，在抑郁、偏执与精神错乱的主题框架下展开歌词叙事。专辑融合了 Porcupine Tree、Steve Wilson 式的合成器美学与简约主义的重复手法，但在创新性上更偏向对既有风格谱系的整合而非突破，跨界融合涵盖新浪潮、流行摇滚与艺术摇滚的多个面向。

items.body: Valencia label Industrial Complexx reissues the various-artists compilation “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends” on double cassette and digital on October 15, 2026. The 18-track set, originally released by Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, gathers international minimal synth, electro-punk and industrial acts covering the catalogue of Suicide’s Alan Vega and Martin Rev. SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends by Various Artists The reissue accompanies the Spanish-language publication of “Suicide, delincuentes electrónicos,” an essay on the band by musician and writer Pedro Peñas y Robles, originally published in French and English in 2024 and now released in Spanish by Industrial Complexx. The book traces the duo’s genesis and the chaotic sessions behind their 1977 debut album, drawing on testimony from scene figures including Marc Hurtado of Étant Donnés. ‘SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends’ contributors The tribute pairs Vega and Rev’s original catalogue with reinterpretations from Distel, Radical G, The Horrorist, David Carretta and Jürgen Engler of Die Krupps, Növö, Adan+Ilse featuring Gabi Delgado of D.A.F., Marc Hurtado performing with Alan Vega himself, Liebknecht featuring Kristoffer Grip of Agent Side Grinder, Unknown Celebrities, Laag, Position Parallele, Cruise [ctrl] featuring Richard 23 and Patrick Codenys of Front 242, The Present Moment, Absolute Body Control, Millimetric featuring Dirk Da Davo of The Neon Judgement, Black Egg featuring hausfrau, Simi Nah featuring KGB, and In Death It Ends featuring Usher of Norma Loy. Covered songs include “Che,” “Ghost Rider,” “Cheree,” “Frankie Teardrop,” “Dream Baby Dream” and “Diamonds, Fur Coat, Champagne.” Industrial Complexx describes the collection as channeling “the same abrasive, alienating and futuristic energy” that shaped Suicide’s catalogue. About Suicide Suicide was an American duo formed in New York City in 1970 by vocalist Alan Vega and instrumentalist Martin Rev, initially a trio with guitarist Paul Liebgott before continuing as a two-piece. The group paired Vega’s stream-of-conscious, rockabilly-inflected vocals with Rev’s minimal synthesizer and drum-machine backing, and was among the first acts to use the term “punk music” to describe itself, in 1970. Suicide independently released its debut album, “Suicide,” in 1977 on Red Star Records, featuring “Ghost Rider,” “Frankie Teardrop” and “Cheree.” A second album, “Suicide: Alan Vega and Martin Rev,” followed in 1980 on Ze Records, then “A Way of Life” in 1988, “Why Be Blue” in 1992 and the final studio album, “American Supreme,” in 2002. Vega and Rev also worked separately: Vega collaborated with Andrew Eldritch of The Sisters of Mercy as The Sisterhood in 1986, and with Alex Chilton and Ben Vaughn on “Cubist Blues” in 1996, while both released solo albums throughout their careers. Suicide played its final concert at London’s Barbican Centre on July 9, 2015, before Alan Vega died on July 16, 2016, at age 78. “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends,” first released via Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, returns via Industrial Complexx on October 15, 2026, alongside the Spanish edition of Pedro Peñas y Robles’s book on the band.

items.body: One half of the Senior Staff was able to get out to a wholly non-ID:UD related gig over the weekend and catch Calgary’s Mares Of Thrace play a very rhythmically tight and cathartic set of doom metal. As we’ve briefly discussed here and there we’re both fans of a decent amount of metal covering a number of sub-genres, but neither of us are experts. Frankly, sometimes its nice to switch off the part of your brain that needs to be developing informed opinions and producing thoughtful analysis at all times and just enjoy some music simply because you dig it. But speaking of thoughtful analysis (?), let’s get you back to the home front with this week’s tracks. Dismantled Godflesh, “Master And Slave” Justin Broadrick announced earlier this year that he’d be winding Godflesh down for a second time some fifteen-odd years after its reactivation, but was planning two full LPs of new material before that time comes. The first such record sees release on Friday, and while the ratio of dub, electronic, and breaks elements which have always flitted about Godflesh releases had perhaps increased over the last few post-reunion albums, it’s hard not to think that Decay will be going right for the jugular Streetcleaner style based on its opening track. Turn it up and revel in the soothing annihilation of that bass tone. Decay by GODFLESH Grendel, “Dominion” It’s somehow been 7 years since the release of Grendel’s last LP Ascending the Abyss. It’s been a tangible absence in Our offices; JD Tucker has spent the last decade and a half redefining his legacy as an electro-industrial stylist and producer, starting with 2012’s genre-defying Timewave: Zero and the superlative Age of the Disposable Body, the latter being legitimately one of the most important political albums of the 2010s in Our Thing. “Dominion” speaks to the band we’ve come to know Grendel to be while showing some intriguing developments, such as JD’s now accomplished melodic vocal style, some very smooth string programming and sleek modern sound design applied to a classic EBM gallop. All that and lyrics that don’t just decry the social media era but examine the panopticon of control they emerge from? Welcome back Grendel, we missed you. Dominion by Grendel Dismantled, “Zero” Speaking of long-awaited returns, holy shit, there’s new Dismantled. Gary Zon’s long-running project has always been a standard bearer for a version of hard and harsh electro-industrial that maintains the genre’s atmospheric and emotional core. The first track from the forthcoming Endless is “Zero”, a cut that features Zon’s distinctive processed and multi-layered vocals, samples, and some fine string programming for good measure. It’s melancholic, but after a more than half a decade wait (the album was originally teased all the way back in 2021), it’s a sound that feels right. Endless by Dismantled Rosetta Stone, “Shadowban” Porl King’s moved Rosetta Stone through a number of preceding modes since reactivating the legendary second wave of goth rock project as a solo joint seven years back. A forthcoming release looks to keep that trend going (the Executing Nostalgia title feels rather on the nose in that regard) – one half of it will be made up of classic goth covers, continuing in the tradition of Unerotica and last year’s Nothing Is Sacred, while the other half is originals. This first taste of the latter feels like a callback to a very different moment in King’s history, though: the claustrophobic and hazy bass fog of this cut’s a dead ringer for the post witch house loops and grooves which made up the bulk of the voluminous In Death It Ends catalog in the 2010s. Shadowban by Rosetta Stone Control Fields, “Black Anomaly” Some solidly chewy bass sits at the centre of the B-side of the debut single from Tbilisi producer Control Fields, but that’s not the only thing which has us flashing back to 90s EBM and dark electro. The combo of icy programming and classic “hacking the Gibson” style sampling on this goes down as smooth as a Jolt cola being slammed during an all night Quake LAN party. Friction Code by Control Fields Emmon, “Relics (Kris Baha remix)” Kris Baha is one of the most reliable producers that emerged from the techno-body moment, with his canny grasp of gnarly sound design and how to assemble peak time bangers making him a go-to remixer for many artists. For evidece of why and the results why not check out Baha’s mix for Emmon’s “Relics”, taking the pensive and punchy original and giving it a slick peak-time makeover that references breakbeat driven 90’s techno, some psytrance, and some seriously warped synthwork. This’ll singe your nosehairs if you aren’t careful, play loud with caution. The post Tracks: September 21st, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 本篇为周度单曲推荐合辑，涵盖多支工业与电子场景的近期作品。Godflesh以回归Slab/cajun式厚重贝斯音色开局，新专辑《Decay》首曲延续dub与电子元素的传统，同时以重型贝斯主导听觉冲击。Grendel时隔七年回归，JD Tucker在《Dominion》中展现成熟的旋律化人声处理与EBM经典节拍，歌词层面深入剖析社交媒体时代的全景监控权力结构。Dismantled的《Zero》则延续硬派电工业路线，通过多层处理人声与弦乐编程在压抑中铺陈忧郁情绪。文章语言风格随性但信息密度高，对作品历史脉络与音乐细节均有交代，是面向工业/EBM受众的实用推荐。

items.body: A veteran of groundbreaking music-video and visual collaborations, Ben Stokes puts his most personal stamp on Dimensional Holophonic Sound (DHS), his singular project blending acid electronics, old-school analog imagery, and experimental video production. Simultaneously, Stokes has built a distinctive career at the intersection of sound, art, technology, and visuals. Inside Ben Stokes’ vinyl obsession Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Benjamin Stokes could exist solely as a collaborator with other artists and his resume would remain an envious one. He has directed music videos for giants like Nine Inch Nails, Public Enemy, Ministry, The Orb and Meat Beat Manifesto, the latter of which he’s also a band member alongside industrial dance music pioneer Jack Dangers, whom Stokes additionally collaborates with in another outfit called Man From Mantis. He has created visuals for DJ Shadow‘s live sets, directed hype video for the Dallas Cowboys, and even helped pull off the feat of M.I.A. and Janelle Monae performing as holograms at each other’s live shows, simultaneously, on opposite coasts of the United States. And this is only a small scratch on his winning lottery ticket of collaborations. Dimensional Holofonic Sound (DHS) however, is singularly Ben Stokes. “I love collaborating with people but I think every artist needs a solo project,” he says. “Something that is their own signature and unique flavor.” I spoke with Stokes—ironically as he took a break from creating visuals for DJ Shadow‘s upcoming Endtroducing 30th Anniversary tour—to talk about his new DHS album, Concept Record, AI art, love of acid music, and any upcoming plans for live shows. “[Concept Record] is kind of like a big love letter to vinyl itself,” says Stokes. “I mean, the concept is, ‘The record is the concept.’ It’s all about vinyl. It’s an art object. I went to art school and I was trained to make objects, so it was very important to me.” That love of records is so grand that he took a risk, spent the extra money on the bells and whistles—including fifteen lock-groove loop tracks—and wrote his love letter on a hand-crafted double-vinyl edition of the album engineered with Anne-Marie Suenram of Suenram Productions in San Pablo, California, the only woman-owned and operated cutting and mastering company of its kind in North America. Ben Stokes and Anne-Marie Suenram engineering the lacquer cut for the vinyl edition of Concept Record. Taken from Stokes’ Instagram page. Locking into the groove :: Cutting the vinyl with its special features was a true labor of love. “It was indeed a major learning experience that challenged me to apply everything I’d learned,” Suenram says via email, “but with Ben‘s encouragement I was able to figure out what I needed to do. Ben‘s record was, and still is, the only record I’ve done with this kind of cut,” she says. “I wanted to try to do all the kind of physical, fun things that you can do only with vinyl,” Stokes continues, “like lock-grooves, beat matching and putting things at 133.33 beats per minute, which if you look at those tracks that are at that tempo, the grooves on the physical record actually kind of line up in an interesting visual way. And um, little side note, the inner disk labels, if you set your phone to 30 frames a second [and record a video] you get some semblance of a little animation there.” Honing in specifically on the logistics of creating a record with so many lock-groove tracks, Stokes brought along a favorite record from his collection called 500 Lock-Grooves By 500 Artists as a template. “Anywhere you drop the needle, it locks. [Suenram] looked at that record under a microscope and she was like, ‘I’m not sure how they did this, and we can’t do it quite this way with my machinery,'” Stokes explains. “The workaround was to create sort of like an entry ramp onto a freeway,” he says, “so there’s a little silence before each lock groove, and then it locks. It circles in on itself. And you really can’t test it, so you don’t really know if it’s going to work until you get your test pressings and at that point, I was like, well, I’m not going back.” Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Signature Ben Stokes kind of stuff :: Lucky for him, as well as for us, it worked very well and serves as another feature of the record’s concept, which is mixing the two records with each other—or with other records—on turntables. Stokes has done DJ sets with the album already, using his 500 Lock-Grooves record alongside Concept Record, and says they worked perfectly together. “Every lock groove on any record will match up with any lock groove on any other record, if you’re playing at the same speed.” He encourages musicians and DJs to post their own mixes to Instagram. “I would love to see what people do,” he says excitedly. All of these nifty features would be mere window dressing without solid DHS music at the core. “I didn’t want it to overshadow that it’s also a new DHS record,” says Stokes. “Part of it came about because I stumbled into a really funny sample, and it’s basically like [a celebrity] interviewing himself, and he’s talking about his album, and he’s like, ‘Oh, it’s just a great album. I mean, it’s what they call a concept record.’ So, that kind of sent me in that trajectory… led me down a rabbit hole. After that initial, like, kind of inspiration, then I just threw in every sample that I have of people talking about records. It’s got some acid house tracks and some minimal electronic-y stuff. I don’t know, signature Ben Stokes kind of stuff.” A good portion of Concept Record is dedicated to the acid music style DHS is known for. From dropping the “Green Acid” and subsequently being treated in the “Hospital Tent,” to the reminder of “I Can Feel It,” blooping along with “Supersonic Holofonic,” then flashing back with “Cut To Black” and “Full Blackout,” the whole middle section plays like one big, aural, acid-trip. “Yeah, there is kind of like a little storyline there,” admits Stokes. When asked what draws him to the style, he replies, “It was seminal. I went to school in Chicago in 1986, and the whole house thing was just teetering into acid. I don’t even think the term acid in 1986 was prevalent. But I was schooled on that stuff through WBMX radio in Chicago where, literally, I mean, the entire city would be listening to the same station. You’d hear it coming out of cars. On your front stoop, you’d hear it, one car going by with the Doppler effect, and you’d hear another one on the same station come in the other direction. I mean, it was just such a magical time. I was so young and that music was just totally new and unlike anything else that I had ever heard. I already loved electronic stuff, but this was just like, wow, these endless mixes of pretty much anonymous stuff WBMX would play for 4 hours on Friday and Saturday night. So that was just a really formative time for me. Definitely a really cool time, I think, for music.”   Redefining The Concept Record :: Now 40 years removed from those halcyon college days, the imagery Stokes has created for Concept Record‘s gatefold cover is decidedly 2026. While the content of many of the pictures may evoke the 1950s and 1960s in style, the artificial intelligence used to create them, as well as the music video for the album’s title track, “Concept Record​,” is apparent. “I actually hate AI,” Stokes says. “If I had found some film about a company that made a shiny silver record and everyone was analyzing it, I’m sure I would have used that.” He underscores that working in the industry he’s in, often being called in by companies as an art director for audio/visual projects, “You gotta keep up with the new tools. I spent a year just learning how to use some of the AI tools.” For Stokes it’s a reflection of this moment in time, yet he still tried to approach it from a familiar standpoint. “In a lot of ways, these images for the cover and for that video were very much like creating stock footage from possibly old educational films or something like that. I just created them in a very different way,” he says. “But it felt kind of familiar territory for me because I was thinking of it like stock footage.” Don’t expect AI creation to be the new norm for Stokes though. “You mentioned the ‘Supersonic [Holofonic]’ video,” he says, which I indeed had. “Well, that’s all found-footage. That’s very DHS.” He continues, “I’m sure that I will use [AI] again for work things, but when it comes to DHS stuff I think I’m going old school for everything going forward. It was an interesting detour and I feel like that’s something that, as an artist, I do often,” he says. “I did that video, I did this album cover, and then I canceled all my subscriptions. I’m going back to my roots. I like going outside with my camera and shooting stuff or doing stop motion animation. And I think that people are kind of probably craving a little bit more rough-around-the-edges analog look, you know?” Stokes stresses as to the musical content, “I did put a very big disclaimer on the inside that no audio was created using AI.”   The Art of the Tease :: With Concept Record being Ben Stokes‘ ode to the vinyl record, it almost begs the question as to what he’s been spinning lately. “I’ve been really getting into 45s,” he says. “I go up to my mom’s cabin in northern Minnesota and there’s like this thrift store called Rick’s Relics in Tower, Minnesota, and they just have this phenomenal collection of records. Just boxes and boxes and piles that, you know, they’re all out of their sleeves. It’s like 25 cents for a 7-inch. And I’ve been picking up all kinds, like The Trashmen, a Minneapolis band from the 60s. They’re, like, garage surf sort of style. I love a lot of that shit.” In continuing to answer the same question, Stokes pivots to Meat Beat Manifesto. “I absolutely love everything Jack [Dangers] does. I think it’s just incredible.” He admits to a little name dropping on his album. “I had to name-call Meat Beat Manifesto by naming a song, “Meat Beat Manifesto Soundcheck.” That was us at a show, doing soundcheck for a show.” Casually in the conversation Stokes drops a bombshell: “There is going to be a Meat Beat Manifesto tour early next year.” Cue the sound of a needle scratching across a record. “We’re booked to do a couple shows in Europe, and then there’s going to be some dates here [in the U.S.]. And, um, more info to come! And at some point, Jack and I are going to do probably a [Man From] Mantis album. Sometime in the, uh, indefinite future,” he teases. Does this mean new Meat Beat material is around the corner? “Yeah, well, Jack‘s always, always got new stuff coming out,” is the response. What of a DHS live tour supporting Concept Record though? “Well, I would love to,” says Stokes. “I’m trying to figure out a stealthy version that I can fit in the trunk of my car and like, you know, do at least a small mini tour. LA, I think, is pretty conceivable. And of course, when we do shows locally here in San Francisco, I get the absolute pleasure of having Jack performing with me as DHS.” You might guess what Stokes offers next: “I’m just going to have to keep you posted on that.” Perhaps Ben Stokes just came up with his next concept: The Art of the Tease. If so, it’s coming along nicely. Concept Record is available on Bandcamp. Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound    The post Chit Chat with Ben Stokes of Dimensional Holofonic Sound first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 本乐评以访谈形式介绍Ben Stokes的个人项目Dimensional Holofonic Sound（DHS）及其专辑《Concept Record》。Stokes长期从事音乐视频与视觉艺术创作，曾为Nine Inch Nails、Public Enemy、DJ Shadow等艺术家执导影像，并参与M.I.A.与Janelle Monae的全息同步演出项目。《Concept Record》是他对黑胶唱片这一介质的致敬之作，以手工制作的双黑胶版本呈现，包含十五条锁纹循环音轨，强调唱片的实体艺术属性。母带处理由旧金山湾区的女性独立工作室Suenram Productions完成，采用独特的切割工艺。整体内容融合酸电子、模拟成像与实验影像制作，跨界属性鲜明。

We have electro with Cultivated Electronics, To Pikap and Shipwrec, and breaks with DjRum and Withhold. Two hours of nonsensical anecdotes and lots of great music. Two hours of nonsensical anecdotes and lots of great music And now, we’re back after the summer. I spent most of August in Ireland, and the inspiration for this edition comes from my little country. We have music from Dublin with Poseidon84 and Industrial Lies, although I sadly missed the label night this year in Dublin. Another source of ideas, also from Ireland, is Blindboy‘s podcasts, and this month we explore references between house and techno. items.body: Kommission Z80 is a Swedish duo that, following a debut album released on Electric Underground Records, is now self-releasing its second opus. I don’t recall ever hearing anything by them before, but these 13 tracks provide a clear picture of the duo’s musical identity. Their primary influences clearly lie within the realm of old-school EBM—specifically the kind of EBM characterized by thoughtful composition and well-crafted arrangements. The vocals, and indeed some of the tracks, remind me somewhat of Portion Control, while other songs reveal traces of Skinny Puppy’s influence. One track even feels like a nod to Front 242. It should be noted that these are all bands with highly distinctive sounds and complex structures. Kommission Z80 doesn’t quite reach that level yet; they would benefit from improving some technical aspects, particularly the mixing and recording. Nevertheless, there is undeniable potential here. Several strong tracks are waiting to be discovered, and the latter part of the album, in particular, features some very cool songs. Kommission Z80 is a name that true EBM enthusiasts should remember. (Rating:7). Listen to “Here Comes The Consequences”: Here Comes The Consequences by Kommission Z80 About Kommission Z80 Kommission Z80 is a Swedish duo from Borås formed by Erik Holmberg and Fredrich Legnemark, working in an old-school EBM style. The project’s debut single “Empire” arrived in 2024 through Electric Underground Records, followed by the debut album “Hegemony” and the “Reasonable Conclusions” EP in 2025. “Sic Semper Tyrannis” is the duo’s self-released 2026 follow-up.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自瑞典双人组，是他们独立发行的第二张全长作品，包含十三首曲目。整体取向扎根于老派EBM传统，编曲注重层次与结构感，主唱的处理方式让人联想到Portion Control，部分段落带有Skinny Puppy的影子，个别曲目甚至向Front 242致敬。在制作层面，混音与录音质量仍有改进空间，尚未达到那些经典乐队的高度，但创作潜力清晰可辨。专辑后半部分收录了多首质量出色的作品，整体呈现出克制而有力的工业电子质感。对于长期关注EBM与暗潮场景的听众而言，这个名字值得留意。

items.body: I went to bed I saw you there You shook your head It’s all out, where? There is a special cruelty in being wounded by someone who has already left the room. The accusation lands, the door closes, and suddenly one person possesses the luxury of departure while the other inherits everything that remains unresolved. They replay every sentence, defend themselves to an empty room, and search for the words they were never allowed to speak. Kind Kid’s latest single bleed inhabits precisely that imbalance, turning abandonment into a bright, brisk synthpop song whose surface seems almost indecently cheerful beside the injury underneath. The arrangement draws its movement from eighties synthpop and its darker hues from the gothic electronics of Clan of Xymox to the Modern Darkwave sensibilities of Boy Harsher, with eerie synth flourishes and cold, uneasy tones curling around a dark disco beat. The rhythm keeps the song moving toward the dance floor, though something in those keyboards suggests the argument will be waiting when you get home. Julien Martinez sings from the position of someone denied the final word, his sense of injury finding an accomplice in the music’s disquiet. That tension gives “bleed” its emotional force: the hooks offer release while the synths keep returning to the bruise. The lyrics are deliberately circular. Images return, phrases repeat, and the speaker seems trapped inside an encounter that has ended everywhere except in his own mind. Repetition becomes psychological rather than decorative, suggesting those arguments one continues hours later while washing dishes, driving home, or staring at the ceiling, inventing increasingly perfect replies for someone who is no longer listening. “I thought of it as some metaphorical situation where someone’s been left behind after some sort of attack… left to “bleed,” muses Kind Kid frontman Julien Martinez. “Sometimes a situation can feel so much different to one person than the other.” One person may regard an argument as a momentary discharge of anger; the other can experience the same exchange as an injury requiring days to understand. bleed catches that disparity without weighing down its pop architecture. Its hooks remain airy, almost playful, while the words circle rejection, exposure, and helplessness. Listen to bleed below and order the single here. bleed by kind kid Recorded at Golden Dice Studios in Brooklyn, the track was produced by Dutchrevz and Kind Kid, then mixed and mastered by Michele Ricci. bleed is Kind Kid’s final single before the album arrives October 9th. items._cn_summary: Kind Kid的单曲《bleed》探讨了被留下的人独自面对未解决冲突的心理状态——一方已离去，另一方却被困在不断回响的争论中。歌词刻意采用循环结构，重复的意象映射出人们在洗碗、开车、凝视天花板时仍继续组织回击话语的精神内耗。音乐层面上，歌曲以明亮的合成器流行表面承载深层的伤痕，编曲借鉴八十年代合成器流行的节奏律动，同时融入Clan of Xymox的哥特电子色调与Boy Harsher的现代暗潮质感，冷冽的合成器纹理缠绕在暗色迪斯科节拍之上。Julien Martinez的人声定位于被剥夺最后发言权的位置，旋律钩子提供释放感，而合成器层则不断折返至伤痛本身。歌曲捕捉到同一事件在两人之间感知的巨大落差：一方视之为一时之气，另一方则经历数日才能理解的创伤。

items.body: Are we better off alone Will I come into my own Are we better off alone Being understood by someone is a comfort until the relationship ends and their imagined opinion starts conducting an inspection of everything wrong with you. Boy Harsher’s Faulty inhabits that uncomfortable interval between asking to be wanted and wondering what that wanting has cost. Jae Matthews sings as though the verdict may already be in, while Augustus Muller gives her doubts enough room to move. The question of being better off alone becomes something to turn over on the dancefloor, where thinking clearly has always been optional. The song accompanies the release of Get Mean, out now following its September 18 arrival through Atlantic Records. Their first album since 2022’s The Runner, the twelve-track record follows the end of Matthews and Muller’s romantic relationship in early 2024, after a period of family loss, personal upheaval, and creative uncertainty. Continuing the band meant finding a way to work together while the terms of their lives were changing. That makes the tenderness of Faulty particularly affecting: the people making this music understand how complicated its questions can become. A kicking beat, busy hi-hats, and quivering synths set Faulty in motion. Its dark disco rhythm has some of Careful’s physical insistence, softened by broad synth pads and little descending electronic notes that drop through the arrangement with a rounded, almost playful boop. When the beat pauses to breathe, the synths take on a Vangelis-like warble, briefly opening the song into something more spacious and cinematic. The rhythm returns beneath a lead synth that bends up and down in pitch, while Matthews keeps her voice hushed and close, breathing the words with a tenderness that borders on resignation. The lyrics put affection and self-assessment in an uncomfortable room together. Asking whether she is faulty gives another person the power to diagnose her; asking whether she will come into her own begins to take some of that power back. Repetition keeps either possibility from becoming a settled conclusion. Matthews sounds caught between wanting to be held and recognizing how much of herself might be waiting outside the relationship. Directed by Boy Harsher and shot on 35mm with cinematography by Owen Smith-Clark, the final video in the Get Mean series returns to a room lined in brown wood paneling. A television glows blue on a black stand, a small fan sits by the window, and a microphone cable trails across the carpet. Against that ordinary setting, the changing cast look dressed for entirely different evenings: a white cowboy hat, metallic bodysuits, striped knitwear, black boots. Each person seems to have brought a private version of the same bad night. The camera moves from fixed views of the room into close-ups of faces, hands, and bodies moving past one another. People share the frame, lean together, or briefly touch, but proximity never quite settles the question in the chorus. There is a lovely awkwardness to it: the self-consciousness of dancing at home, followed by the sudden absorption of forgetting you are being watched. By the end, the people have gone and the television is still there. The room has held all that feeling without offering anyone an answer. Watch the video for Faulty below: Across Get Mean, the effort to keep going takes several musical forms. Writing began to move again when Matthews took to the road, travelling through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest, and South Florida. The album was eventually recorded in eight locations across the United States, Mexico, and Italy, its unsettled circumstances allowing new sounds and approaches into the duo’s work. Matthews describes it as “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” The three singles we covered ahead of its release made clear how much that offering could contain. The first indication came with Jeans, released in June. Its springy guitar figure and bubbling electronics brought a new wave directness to Boy Harsher, with a steel-slide twang giving the song a western accent. Our earlier comparison to the Pretenders still fits the way Matthews’ cool delivery rides that guitar, while the buoyancy also suggests Muller’s work in Safe Mind. Beneath the cheek is a sharp little study of ambition: the dream of escaping a small town, the dream of becoming somebody, and the possibility of ending up selling an image of freedom by the pair. The band’s latex line-dancing video, conceived with Robert Palmer’s Addicted to Love in mind, makes that collision between aspiration, performance, and merchandise deliciously literal. Hard Beat, unveiled alongside July’s album announcement, tightens the pressure around a repeating bass-synth figure and an unrelenting kick. As we noted then, there is something of Depeche Mode’s Behind the Wheel in its meeting of motion, desire, and surrendered control. Matthews moves between confession and invitation while the rhythm keeps pushing ahead. Its video makes those exchanges physical through an elaborate leg brace, a Cadillac, and a handheld camcorder, drawing medical hardware, automotive controls, and the invasive act of filming into the same uneasy visual language. Within the album, the track preserves the severe club momentum that has long served Boy Harsher so well, giving the softer and more openly melodic songs something solid to push against. August’s Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call) puts a warmer arrangement around the indignity of waiting for someone to remember you exist. A brisk new wave beat, rounded bass, bright keyboards, and short bursts of distorted guitar carry Matthews’ unhappy drawl toward the sort of pop chorus that can make despair briefly feel sociable. Her insistence that she is okay sounds increasingly like something she needs to practice. Our earlier review followed that idea into the lyric video, where yellow karaoke lettering crosses the blue screen of a CRT television. Created with vintage video equipment by Sean McGuirk and shot by Jesse Korman, it turns failed communication into a singalong with nobody else visibly present. Heard beside Faulty, the song makes the eventual question of solitude feel earned. Coming Home opens with Matthews in a smoky, Lynchian register, her voice suspended over steadily repeating synths and a breezy dance beat. The low guitar tones bring New Order to mind, with the melodic weight of a Peter Hook bassline translated onto guitar. That combination gives the song an appealing pull between bodily ease and emotional uncertainty. The rhythm leaves the windows open; the vocal suggests someone still deciding whether it is safe to come inside. Here, the album’s broader musical interests allow vulnerability to sound inviting without making it seem simple. Ice Pick (Walk Away) makes a particularly satisfying turn toward gothic rock. The parenthetical invites a Sisters of Mercy comparison before the guitar has even had its say, and the melody strengthens the association with their First and Last and Always period. A deep post-punk bass groove and the crunchy splash of the drum machine give the track a familiar dry ice chill. Matthews’ tender delivery moderates that severity, placing a vulnerable voice inside an arrangement with its collar firmly turned up. The resemblance is a pleasure to hear, especially from a duo whose love of this music has often been expressed through a different set of instruments. Pray 4 Me lets the bass loosen its hips. Soft synth pads, a sexy funk groove, and quivering bell tones bring a strain of Bryan Ferry-eque sophisti-pop into the album, expanding its capacity for pleasure as well as distress. There is a suppleness to the arrangement that makes this feel like a natural extension of the record’s emotional dynamic range. Desire, after all, does not become less complicated when somebody gives it a particularly good bassline. Boy Harsher sounds comfortable letting elegance and appetite share the same song. The album closes with Bleed, setting trip-hop beats against crystalline synths and low, bone-marrow-churning bass. Imagine the Bristol-born genre taking shape inside the electric dreams of the mid-1980s: the drums with a twitching hi-hat and thump have that low, unhurried weight, while the electronics give the space around them a cool, glassy clarity. After the movement of the preceding songs, this slower finish lets the record exhale. Its change of pace offers a place to sit with everything that has happened. Get Mean gives Matthews and Muller’s affection for post-punk, synthpop, goth, and dance music considerably more room to misbehave. They have grown as people, their lives have changed, and their music has had the good sense to evolve. Those expecting Pain on an endless loop, or Careful with a fresh set of track titles, may find this development inconvenient. For listeners who share Jae and Gus’s musical curiosity, there is pleasure in hearing them loosen up, follow their enthusiasms, and discover what this new chapter of their partnership can become. And if Get Mean isn’t the Boy Harsher you ordered, well, tough shit. Listen to Get Mean below and order the album here. Additional listening and purchase options are available here. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Since forming in 2014, Matthews and Muller have taken Boy Harsher from the small cassette run of Lesser Man, whose Pain spread widely online, through Yr Body Is Nothing in 2016, the Country Girl EP in 2017, and Careful in 2019. Their background in film became central to 2022’s The Runner, which they wrote, produced, directed, and scored. Their work in cinema also includes The Lonely Woman, their debut feature as directors, starring Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, and Sturgill Simpson. Boy Harsher’s The Heartbreak Tour resumes September 25 at Basilica Hudson, with North American dates running through November 5 at New York’s Knockdown Center. The European and UK run begins November 14 in Lyon and includes London’s Roundhouse on November 29. Choir Boy joins select dates. Visit the band’s shows page for tickets and current availability. items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items._genre: avant-garde jazz / vocal improvisation / experimental piano
items._cn_summary: Ran Blake与Dominique Eade合作的《Roots & Byways》以极端的选材逻辑著称：Max Roach的硬波普、Mingus的爵士写作、Whitney Houston的流行金曲、Michel Legrand的香颂在这些曲目中并列呈现，揭示出旋律骨架下隐藏的共通结构。Blake不做传统意义上的诠释，而是将作品拆解至最小单元，使熟悉的素材呈现出近乎陌生的面貌。Eade的演唱是该专辑区别于Blake与Jeanne Lee经典合作的支点，她跳出Billie Holiday式的克制，以逐音节雕琢歌词的方式塑造高度个人化的演绎，同时将饱满的喜悦注入那些带有黑色电影质感的曲目。这种对唱法路径的偏离使整张作品既属于Blake的美学谱系，又展现出独立的感染力。

items.body: Richard J. Birkin’s official soundtrack to Jon McGregor’s Reservoir 13 was written, performed, and recorded live with Haiku Salut, an instrumental trio from the English Midlands. The book was awarded the 2017 COSTA Novel of the Year, and its soundtrack wears the same shoes; its blue threads help in framing a photograph of sudden loneliness, its strings wrapped up in midwinter mystery. Described by The Guardian as ‘a chilling meditation on loss and time’, Reservoir 13’s soundtrack is equally cool-blooded. The strings search for missing 13-year-old Rebecca, the sudden loss of light shrivelling the music into a sluggish state of shock. The unexplained and instantaneous earthquake, an event as cataclysmic as the one in Don DeLillo’s Point Omega, sends an endless ripple through tomorrow. Everyone’s looking for answers – crime or no crime – but life doesn’t work like that; the Universe isn’t required to offer a neat resolution or a form of closure. For the most part, things drift. People drift. Unexpected, and often terrible, events happen each and every day. Threads often just run out, with no explanation given, and no end to suffering in sight. No resolving. But, for Birkin, this is potent material. Strings swell slowly, and that gives the music more of an edge. Paradoxically, an unstoppable force, screaming at the top of its lungs, can be felt inside the quiet, caressing motion of the bow. A muted scream. Whenever McGregor was at a book reading, Birkin’s technology allowed the writer access to the phones in the audience, creating a communal experience as the reciting of words, along with an unfolding section of the story, met with audience participation – and, of course, this produced a number of different outcomes. Not one reading was ever the same. The piano has always lent itself to deep pools of thought and sliding melancholia, but in this case it’s gut-wrenching, less a sole tear or an escaping trickle from the eye and more an inconsolable aching. The music disappears, too. Physically present but mentally gone, haunted by an ongoing and incredibly traumatic event, the music seems to be preoccupied with this all-consuming grief, hardly able to process pain as the crushing weight of the strings continue to bear down upon the creaking stave. The residents are trapped in a horrific situation, and the melody can’t find a way to break out of its minor key, either. The single piano motif is important, as it seems to represent isolation, a singular sorrow, a loneliness and an inability to do anything about anything. Later, strings join the search party, weeping along with the piano. Life has to go on, but a sick mood hangs over the land. The soundtrack is heavy, but that only makes it all the more powerful. Soundtracks are often only reserved for film, although listeners have, in the past, been blessed with book-scores, like those in The Book Report series, so this somewhat novel (excuse me) approach is an area that can be further explored. Film will always offer strict representations and the forced digestion of its images, while the book is individual, creating its own imagery for every reader. The reader has to work in order to create the world. Likewise, music is subjective, too, but the book’s theme ensures sober music. The book’s meditation on loss requires a deep sensitivity, and Birkin ushers the strings to appropriate, and respectful, places, the piano gently bleeding from its emotional wounds. www.rjbirkin.bandcamp.com

Birkin与器乐三重奏Haiku Salut为Jon McGregor同名小说创作的配乐，演奏与录音均以现场方式完成。整张作品以弦乐与钢琴为核心载体，弦乐缓慢膨胀并搜索叙事裂缝，钢琴则反复呈现单一动机，象征孤独与无解的悲伤。弦乐在低音区的持续施压配合小调的封闭感，构筑出压抑的冬季氛围。此外，Birkin在McGregor的读书会中曾运用技术手段将听众手机纳入演出，形成文本与音乐互动的现场实验。该作品在配乐概念与现场呈现层面具有一定实验性，但从纯音乐体裁角度更偏向当代古典与电影配乐的交叉地带，与用户偏好的实验电子、暗潮等领域的直接契合度有限。

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由挪威二人组Sudan Dudan创作，属于北欧传统民谣范畴。整张专辑以原声吉他为核心，辅以挪威传统乐器如fiddle、langeleik（挪威古筝）、lyr和口弦，营造出质朴的民间质感。专辑标题意为"黑暗的副歌"，歌词以挪威语书写，涉及大地、太阳、星辰、神话与谜语，体现出对北欧传统的追溯。创作上融入挪威传统的"tralling"人声技法，将旋律以无词音节演绎。末曲加入电吉他，深沉而twang的音色令人联想到Duane Eddy或David Lynch配乐，为传统框架增添了一丝现代张力。整体制作精良，氛围介于沉思与轻盈之间，是一张扎根挪威民间音乐语汇、同时具备一定艺术构想的作品。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以乌克兰被劫持儿童的真实悲剧为主题，将传统民歌与原创作品交织。创作者Marichka是一位乌克兰裔加拿大歌手，她召集了加拿大和乌克兰两组女性音乐人共同录制，乐器以弓弦乐器为主，辅以班杜拉琴和钢琴。专辑中特别邀请了一位曾被劫持后成功返回的16岁马里乌波尔少女演奏双陶笛。歌曲在传统与现代之间游走，既有对祖母一代被送往异乡劳作的历史回望，也有对当代儿童遭绑架现实的控诉。编曲从温柔民谣到激烈呼喊皆有覆盖，人声是核心表达载体，既承载乌克兰仪式歌曲传统，也直面当下战争的残酷现实。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑聚焦圣多美和普林西比这一非洲最小岛国之一在七八十年代的录音，呈现名为Puxa的独特音乐类型。其节奏根源来自非洲葡语区殖民地传统，同时融合了merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga乃至加勒比影响，成分复杂而层次分明。乐评指出该岛虽小且录音资源有限，音乐本身却充满舞蹈驱动力，吉他交织对位、人声与器乐持续呼应，构成可延伸数小时的现场律动。Pedro Lima领衔的乐队展示了闷音吉他在鼓组前的对峙，Sangazuza则突出贝斯与键盘退出后鼓与吉他的原始律动张力。Africa Negra的政治声援曲目也被提及。作为Bongo Joe发行的地下厂牌合辑，提供了难得的非洲边缘岛屿音乐档案视角。

items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

items.body: Black Tape For A Blue Girl and Projekt Records reissue “The Rope” on October 2, presenting the 1986 debut album in a limited edition that pairs the original mix, remastered, with a new 2026 mix by Sam Rosenthal for its 40th anniversary. The 2LP edition is limited to 300 copies on 140-gram vinyl, with LP1 pressed on baby blue vinyl with black splatters and LP2 on transparent blue vinyl with white splatters. A 2CD digipak edition adds seven bonus tracks. Both formats are released via Projekt Records. “The Rope” is Black Tape For A Blue Girl’s debut album, the project Sam Rosenthal built around his songwriting and electronics, with Oscar Herrera on vocals. Each format includes the full 12-track album twice: the original 1986 mix, remastered, and the new 2026 mix. Martin Bowes of Attrition handled the mastering. The 2LP package adds a 16-page lyric and memorabilia fanzine insert plus a sticker; the 2CD edition comes in a 6-panel digipak with a 4-panel photo insert and sticker. The original 1986 tracklist runs: “memory, uncaring friend”, “hide in yourself”, “within these walls”, “the holy terrors”, “end”, “seven days til sunrise”, “the rope”, “the few remaining threads”, “the lingering flicker”, “slow blur”, “the floor was hard but home” and “we return”. The 2CD edition adds seven bonus tracks exclusive to that format: “the lingering flicker (first draft)”, “within these walls (early mix with clarinet)”, “the holy terrors (long)”, “second dream”, “the lingering flicker (isolated violins)”, “within these walls (short with violins)” and “memory, uncaring friend (remix intro)”. Sam Rosenthal on writing ‘The Rope’ Rosenthal, who also founded Projekt Records, described the circumstances that produced the album: “In November ’85, following two years of recording instrumental electronic music, I invited Oscar Herrera to sing two songs on my ISLANDS cassette. A few months later in February of ’86 I left Florida for college in Orange, California. I was 20 years old, feeling isolated, lonely, missing friends back home. In my dorm room that spring I used the school’s Fostex 250 4-track cassette portastudio to record songs with my lyrics and melodies. Writing words for Oscar to sing over my ethereal and ambient music helped me explore those angsty and tangled feelings. The Rope is half vocal and half instrumental. It’s all quite minimal, yet it’s an album listeners still mention as a favorite. Capturing the confusion and darkness I felt at that time remains valid; new listeners connect with it today. I never would have expected that 40 years later The Rope would be listened to and appreciated by new generations. It’s really nice knowing those feelings are timeless, and the music has a place in people’s lives.” Uncut included “The Rope” in its “200 Greatest Goth Albums” feature, describing it as: “The vehicle for the more electronic songwriting of Projekt Records’ founder Sam Rosenthal, brought to life by singer Oscar Herrera’s arch delivery. BTFABG spun a unique thread of ambient darkwave, neoclassical exoticism and dark cabaret on their relatively bare-boned and lo-fi debut album.” The Rope (40th) by Black Tape For A Blue Girl About Black Tape For A Blue Girl Black Tape For A Blue Girl is the project Sam Rosenthal formed in 1986, built around his own songwriting and electronics and centered from the start on the pairing of his instrumental, ambient compositions with vocalists singing his lyrics. “The Rope”, released that year on Projekt Records, the label Rosenthal founded, introduced Oscar Herrera as vocalist alongside contributions from Allan Kraut, Kim Prior, Adam Buhler, Candy Sherlock and Lara Radford. The project’s discography continued through “Mesmerized by the Sirens” (1987), “Ashes in the Brittle Air” (1989), “A Chaos of Desire” (1991), “This Lush Garden Within” (1993), “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” (1996), “As One Aflame Laid Bare by Desire” (1999), “The Scavenger Bride” (2002), “Halo Star” (2004), “10 Neurotics” (2009), “Tenderotics” (2013), “These Fleeting Moments” (2016), “To Touch the Milky Way” (2018) and “The Cleft Serpent” (2021). Projekt has revisited several of these titles as anniversary reissues in recent years, including “The Cleft Serpent” and “Ashes in the Brittle Air” on vinyl, “Mesmerized by the Sirens” on vinyl and double CD, and “As One Aflame Laid Bare by Desire” and “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” in their own anniversary editions. Rosenthal has also continued to release music outside the project, including ambient and drone recordings under his own name. The 40th anniversary edition of “The Rope” extends that reissue campaign to the album that started it, presenting Herrera’s original vocal performances and Rosenthal’s 1986 arrangements alongside his 2026 revisiting of the same material.
items._cn_summary: 这张1986年的首张专辑正值四十周年之际，由Projekt Records推出限量再版，以140克黑胶和2CD两种格式呈现原版混音与2026年新混音的双重版本。Sam Rosenthal以Fostex 250四轨卡带录音机在大学宿舍中构建了这张以太氛围电子为底色、辅以人声的作品，半数为器乐、半数为声乐曲目，制作极简却情感密度极高。Oscar Herrera的人声穿梭于合成器音景与原声乐器之间，黑管与小提琴的加入为暗潮基调添入古典室内乐的质感。2CD版收录七首独家附赠曲目，包含早期混音、孤立的提琴声轨及未发行作品。Martin Bowes负责母带处理，限量300张的蓝色彩溅黑胶附赠歌词纪念册。该作捕捉了创作者二十岁时身处异乡的孤独与困惑，这种情感穿透时间，仍能让当代听众产生共鸣。

items.body: Room of Wires, the UK industrial/electronic duo of two producers who both go by Andrew, released the single “Skin weevil” on September 18, 2026, self-released on Bandcamp. The two-track release pairs the title track with “Do not leave a message” and arrives while the duo works on a new album. Skin weevil by Room of Wires Room of Wires bring an industrial and electronic sound that mixes hard-hitting rhythm programming with the duo’s usual dark ambient textures and field recordings. Both tracks on “Skin weevil” were written and produced by Room of Wires; the cover artwork is by the duo as well, with performance for camera by Fenia Kotsopoulou and photography by Daz Disley. Room of Wires’ ‘Skin weevil’ single The duo has not met in person: one member works with hardware and a tangle of physical wires, the other in software and virtual cables, sharing ideas and sounds over the internet. That process has produced “Skin weevil” as a standalone two-track single rather than part of a longer EP or album, released independently while the pair continue work on their next full-length. No further tracks or release date for that album have been announced. About Room of Wires Room of Wires is a UK industrial/electronic duo of two producers, both named Andrew, who write and record without ever having met, exchanging sounds and ideas remotely. Their debut EP, “Asylum sneaker”, appeared on Section27 in August 2014, followed by the Bandcamp-only “Dead skins” EP in November 2015, “Used as a runner” on Section27 in June 2016, “Black medicine” on Section27 in June 2017, and the remix-featuring “Mastakink” EP, self-released in October 2017. Their debut album, “White transit”, followed in November 2018, and the mini-LP “Test subject” arrived in October 2019. Room of Wires signed to the German label ant-zen for the albums “Plague of people” (April 2021) and “Welcome to the end game” (February 2023), releasing the “Fever switch” EP on Rednetic in October 2021 in between. Further self-released EPs followed with “Floodplains” (November 2023) and the album “If no other means are effective” in December 2025, the duo’s first full-length in close to three years. Alongside their own catalogue, Room of Wires record collaborative material as DasF and Cave like carving, and have contributed remixes and tracks to releases by Ah Cama-Sotz, Flint Glass, 4T Thieves and other acts. “Skin weevil” is their first new material since 2025’s “If no other means are effective”, released as the pair continue work on a new Room of Wires album.
items._cn_summary: Room of Wires 由两位同名为 Andrew 的英国制作人组成，二人从未线下见面，一人专注硬件与实体接线，另一人使用软件与虚拟线缆，通过网络远程交换声音素材完成创作。单曲《Skin weevil》于 2026 年 9 月以自发行形式登陆 Bandcamp，包含标题曲与《Do not leave a message》两首作品，将硬朗的节奏编程与暗氛围质感、现场录音相融合。封面与影像均由组合独立完成，影像部分由 Fenia Kotsopoulou 出演，Daz Disley 负责摄影。这是组合继 2025 年专辑《If no other means are effective》之后的首发新作，作为两张单曲独立发行，而非较长 EP 或专辑的组成部分，预告着下一张全长专辑的制作进程。Room of Wires 长期活跃于 ant-zen 等小众厂牌圈层，作品横跨工业、电子、暗氛围与田野录音的交汇地带。

items.body: Amamere come from Cape Coast, the Fante fishing port where Ebo Taylor and C.K. Mann were born, and they play highlife the way Ghana’s guitar bands played it in the 1970s. Eric Asiedu Agyekum‘s lead guitar sits out front, tenor sax and trumpet play over the top, and behind the kit is Rim Akandoh Jnr, who spent the late 2010s drumming for Taylor. Their live take on “Kokonsani”, the opening track of the 2025 debut Man Shall Be Free on Afro Urban Project, was filmed at Afrika Festival Hertme in the Netherlands on 4 July, during the eight-piece’s first tour outside Ghana. Dominic Ansah plays Ga kpanlogo drums and congas under the kit, and the trumpet belongs to Emmanuel Adjei, grandson of Osibisa‘s Mac Tontoh. Akandoh Jnr’s father, Rim Akandoh, played in Mann’s band before leading the Prince Sparrows Band. Much of the album reworks his songs alongside osode, the fishing-community music Mann electrified, while “Kokonsani”, Twi for a gossip, carries the son’s own lyric. Hear the studio cut of “Kokonsani” HERE and order Man Shall Be Free via THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Amamere – Kokonsani appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: 这支来自加纳海岸角的八人乐队延续了七十年代吉他乐队的高life传统，主奏吉他居前， tenor萨克斯与小号在上方交织，鼓手曾为 Ebo Taylor 效力。鼓手之子 Rim Akandoh Jnr 与小号手 Emmanuel Adjei（Osibisa 乐队 Mac Tontoh 之孙）的家族脉络赋予乐队跨代传承的色彩。专辑 Man Shall Be Free 大多重新演绎其父辈的作品，融合 osode 渔村音乐与高life 电气化语汇，开篇曲 Kokonsani 以特威语歌词指向闲聊八卦。Afrika Festival Hertme 的现场录像捕捉了乐队首次海外巡演的状态，展现了加纳沿海港口城市音乐语汇在当代场景中的延续。

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — Funny how a riff can sound modern, but I guess that's the way it works. Music moves in waves. This album feels very grabby, fresh and now. It's intricately constructed and great-sounding, ready to put any serious home stereo to the test.Where to start? The singing, where this band excels... and that groove! The drums are as much about rhythm as they are about texture. There's plenty of satisfying, head-bang-able metal riffing, paired tightly with great bass work. I'm reminded at times of classic Smashing Pumpkins, so there must be some grunge influence in there as well.The multilayered male/female vocals is a very alluring part of the PRR sound. Their voices don't just blend; they're sculpted together, fused and purposely locked in?creating more of a Beach Boys vibe than casually tagged-on harmonies.There are some definite Pink Floyd-inspired moments here too, particularly in the 12 minute title track 'Terrifying Angels". Then again, maybe I've got it backwards, the PRR take on it could inspire Pink Floyd. Time will tell, but on first listen, I felt I was listening to a masterpiece of modern progressive rock unfold before my ears. It clears out all the cobwebs of stereotypical prog epics and treads boldly into new cinematic textures and possibilities."Terrifying Angels" is a pretty jarring topic to tackle, so it's probably not going to be the "light" entry in the PRR catalogue. And while there's plenty of complexity and detail here, there's also lots of breathing room. But don't get too comfortable in those quieter passages, there's usually some musical surprise waiting around the next corner.Often the song structure seems indecipherable, dragging you at times through room after room of emotional spaces. I love how the familiar can suddenly become strange and new. The lyrics feel important simply because of the way the vocalists are emoting themAnd a shout-out to "Below Radiance," which really shows off Bruce Soord's skills as a mixer, managing all those incredible, epic synth textures without letting the whole thing turn into sonic soup.The last track, "Hold Your Wrath," is 15 minutes long but is a different kind of beast, not an attempt at the epic in a grand way, but a more understated, meditative journey. It features delicate, beautiful, intimate guitar parts, some wonderfully creative drum work, and I love that electronic bass. It feels like another experimental track for the band, though really, the whole album feels adventurous. And despite all of this, you can still bounce to this band.Prog dog score is 4.5 out of 5 dog bones, or 4 out of 5 for the progarchives system.
